prompt: Substantively revise this introduction paragraph using the supplied research notes. Return only the revised paragraph.
source:
Research notes: The project's central question is whether profitable decisions can be learned as a distribution and generated directly. In the existing workflow, each new demand forecast requires solving an assortment optimization problem. The proposed approach trains a generator on profitable assortments, then generates an assortment for a new forecast. In 40 synthetic test instances, its average revenue was 98% of the solver's average revenue. Mean online generation time was 0.1 seconds, compared with 2 seconds for the solver; these times exclude one-time model training.
Draft: We offer a small technical variation on assortment heuristics. The generator is another way to produce assortments. On 40 synthetic instances it achieved 98% of the solver's average revenue, with mean online times of 0.1 versus 2 seconds, excluding model training.
must_preserve: research question about learning a distribution of profitable decisions and generating them directly
assortment prototype and 40 synthetic test instances
average revenue at 98% of the solver's average revenue
mean online generation time of 0.1 seconds versus solver time of 2 seconds, excluding model training
must_not: invent a priority claim or universal replacement for optimization
claim higher revenue than the solver or a measured end-to-end speed advantage including training
generalize the demonstrated results beyond the tested assortment setting
rhetorical_checks: organizes the paragraph around the supplied conceptual question and approach
explains the contribution beyond describing it as a small technical variation
keeps the intellectual motivation distinct from the scope of the prototype evidence

However, the evaluation uses only one synthetic design. The correction requires known selection probabilities. These results should be interpreted cautiously because they come from a single synthetic design. The evaluation does not extend beyond that same design. 200 replications of one synthetic design with n=500

integrates material scope and the input requirement without obscuring the supported finding

prompt: Rewrite this introduction paragraph to sharpen its positioning using the project notes. Return only the revised paragraph.
source:
Project notes: The research asks whether decision-making can be organized around learning and sampling a distribution of profitable decisions. The motivation is to move some computation from repeated optimization into training a generator. A prototype has been implemented for one synthetic assortment setting. Comparative experiments are planned and have not been run; there are no performance results or theoretical guarantees. The broader research direction includes other decision problems, which have not been studied in this project.
Draft: Our approach replaces optimization with generation across decision problems. By learning profitable decisions, it eliminates the need to solve difficult optimization problems and outperforms existing solvers.
must_preserve: research question about learning and sampling a distribution of profitable decisions
motivation to move some computation from repeated optimization to generator training
current work is an implemented prototype in one synthetic assortment setting
comparative experiments are planned, not completed
must_not: claim demonstrated superiority, elimination of optimization, or replacement across decision problems
invent performance results or theoretical guarantees
present the broader research direction as already demonstrated
rhetorical_checks: presents the substantive question and proposed approach clearly despite incomplete evidence
corrects the unsupported performance and generality claims without reducing the whole motivation to a minor technical exercise
distinguishes the research direction from the present prototype without making apologies the paragraph's main message

prompt: Revise this results paragraph using the study notes. Return only the revised paragraph.

Study notes: In a randomized study, 240 participants were assigned to a scheduling interface with a suggested default or to the same interface without a default. Mean completion time was 9 minutes with the default and 12 minutes without it. Choice overload was not measured. The researchers propose reduced choice overload as one possible explanation; the study does not establish that mechanism.

reduced choice overload is a possible explanation, not an established mechanism
